Polyvagal Theory: the basic idea.

Polyvagal Theory is the science of how mammals connect, and how they respond to danger. It links biology to emotion, thought, relationships, and more.

A core piece of the theory is the idea that our bodies can exist in three distinct, evolutionary survival states: safety and social engagement, flight-and-fight mobilization, and shutdown immobilization.

  • WatchPolyvagal Theory for Total Beginners
  • Read“Is Polyvagal Theory Real? Why the 2026 Critique Misunderstands It”
  • DownloadThe Polyvagal One-Pagers (free resource)
The foundation

The three states of the nervous system.

Mammals can be prepared for safety, for mobilization, or for immobilization. These are biological states, not choices.

Safety (ventral vagal)

Active when the external and internal worlds are perceived as safe.

  • Allows for social connection, executive functioning, play, and stillness.
  • Supports health, growth, and restoration.
  • Watch“What Safety Means in the Polyvagal Theory”
  • Read“Polyvagal Safety: What It Is & How to Build It”

Flight & fight (sympathetic)

Survival mode, active when the internal or external worlds are perceived as dangerous. It readies the legs for evasion and the upper body for aggression.

  • Heart rate up, breathing shallow, muscles tense.
  • Attention narrows and scans for danger.
  • Watch“What is Flight/Fight?”
  • ListenFlight/fight podcast episode
  • Read“Anger” blog article

Shutdown (dorsal vagal)

The life-threat response, active when the internal or external worlds are perceived as life threatening. Numbing and dissociation are protective: they open the possibility of escape, and in a genuine life-threat, they blunt physical pain.

  • The body numbs, dissociation sets in.
  • Blood pressure and heart rate drop.
  • Watch“What is Shutdown”
  • ListenShutdown podcast episode
  • ReadThe complete dorsal vagal shutdown guide

If you feel resistance to moving out of a defensive state, it helps to work with polyvagal resistance rather than fighting against it.

Going further

The mixed states.

What happens when more than one of the primary states is active at the same time? You get the mixed states.

Play

Play needs both mammals to have access to their safe and social state and their flight-and-fight state at once. If the flight-and-fight energy becomes too much, it stops being play.

  • Watch“Play or Flight/Fight?”
  • ListenPlay podcast episode
  • ReadBook chapter

Stillness

Stillness is the ability to immobilize, to be still, without fear. It covers lying down to sleep, yoga or meditation, intimacy, using the restroom, and more.

  • Watch“Stillness or Shutdown?”
  • Read“Nervous System Meditation: What It Actually Is”

Freeze

Freeze is its own thing, not just another word for shutdown. Freeze is a tense, rigid immobilization, where shutdown is a collapsed one.

  • Watch“Panic & Rage as Freeze”
  • ListenFreeze podcast episode
  • ReadThe functional freeze guide

Fawn, appease, and intimacy

Fawn, appease, and intimacy are more recent additions to the mixed-state picture, and they leave some interesting open questions. (Fawn is hiding and submissive; appease is fake connection to placate.)

  • Watch“Fawn & Appease”

The vocabulary

Key Polyvagal concepts.

A handful of concepts make the rest of the theory click. They explain how trauma, safety, and regulation actually work in daily life.

The autonomic nervous system

Polyvagal Theory has everything to do with the autonomic nervous system, which regulates all the internal things you don’t think about: breathing, digestion, heart rate. When we move into the primary or mixed states, autonomic shifts take place.

...we are not voluntarily controlling whether we shift in or out of these states.Dr. Stephen Porges
  • Watch“Polyvagal Theory Basics”
  • ReadBook chapter

The Polyvagal Ladder

The Polyvagal Ladder is a metaphor (from Deb Dana) for how the autonomic pathways evolved and function in the mammalian body. Safety pathways sit at the top, flight-and-fight in the middle, and shutdown at the bottom. Autonomic shifts happen in a sequence, not as conscious choices.

We climb up or down the ladder in order. If we detect that we are not safe, we drop into sympathetic arousal: flight first, then fight. If we cannot run and cannot fight, we drop further into shutdown. The reverse is true too: to come out of shutdown, the sympathetic state has to kick in first, a powerful fight, then flight, then back into safety.

  • Watch“Why You Can’t Just Calm Down — The Polyvagal Ladder” (audiobook)
  • Read“Why You Have Resistance to Polyvagal Ladder Climbing”
  • Download“Polyvagal Ladder” sheet

Neuroception

Neuroception is the unconscious detection of cues of danger or safety, in the external or internal environment. It is also what shifts the autonomic states up and down the Polyvagal Ladder.

  • Watch“Neuroception, Explained” (audiobook)
  • Read“Not the Spidey Sense”

Story follows state

The thoughts we have reflect the autonomic state we are in. In a safe and social state, our thoughts are more compassionate and calm. In flight-and-fight, they turn anxious or angry and point outward. In shutdown, they turn apathetic and point inward.

Your autonomic state comes to life and then the information is fed up to your brain, and it’s your brain’s job to make sense of what’s happening in the body, so it makes up a story.Deb Dana, LCSW
  • Watch“You Are Not the Story You Got Stuck In” (audiobook Ep 1)
  • ReadOne-page lesson

The vagal brake

The vagal brake is the influence of the safe and social system on the heart. The stronger the vagal brake, the higher the tolerance to distress. Traumatized people have a compromised social engagement system, so minor problems can become highly triggering events. It’s closely related to what others call the window of tolerance.

  • Watch“The Vagal Brake & the Vagus”
  • ReadBook chapter
An updated model

The Polyvagal Current.

The ladder is a useful first picture, but it shows the states as a sequence you climb one rung at a time.

The Polyvagal Current is my own model. It shows those same three states as a continuous, looping flow instead of a vertical climb: all three active at once, one dominant at a time, with no top, bottom, good, or bad. It’s a different way to see the same theory, not a replacement for the ladder, which stands on its own.

It also changes the question. Instead of asking how to climb back to ventral, the Current asks what happens to a stuck defensive state when you add more safety. The goal was never to live in ventral. It’s to have enough safety in the system that it can move in and out of defense on its own.

  • ReadThe Polyvagal Current, explained in full
  • ReadThe three stuck states: shutdown, freeze, and fight-or-flight
  • ReadHow to read your own nervous system

Why it matters

Polyvagal Theory and trauma recovery.

This is where the theory becomes practical: it reframes what trauma is, and what recovery actually asks of us.

Co-regulation

Mammals are social, and that includes us. We need safe mammals to provide co-regulation. Think of a toddler mid-tantrum: they’re dysregulated, and they need a safe adult in their social engagement system to offer cues of safety. That’s co-regulation.

  • Watch“Trauma & Co-Regulation”
  • Listen“Self & Co-Regulation”
  • Read“How to Reconnect After Trauma”

Mental health and behavioral adaptations

What we call clinical disorders or psychiatric problems may simply be a stuck defensive state, or a behavioral adaptation to being stuck in one. What we commonly call depression may be someone stuck in shutdown. Substance use may be someone’s best attempt at self-regulating a defensive state.

Through the lens of the polyvagal theory, almost every diagnosis in the DSM is a dysregulated nervous system.Deb Dana, LCSW
  • Read“Acting on Impulses vs. Behavioral Adaptations”

The two paths to trauma

Trauma is being stuck in a defensive state. It’s the reaction to the event, not the event itself. It can take two paths.

1. An acute life-threat reaction. Surviving one or more basically one-time events that leave you in a stuck defensive state. Associated with PTSD and the freeze mixed state.

Some examples: war, a school shooting, a car crash, an assault.

2. A chronic disruption of connectedness. Safe, healthy attachment with caregivers or safe others is consistently cut off. Associated with C-PTSD and any of the defensive states.

Some examples: neglect and abuse, ongoing relentless stress, hostage and abuse scenarios, a dangerous neighborhood.

Psychology traditionally approaches trauma through its effects on the mind. This is at best only half the story, and a wholly inadequate one.Peter Levine, PhD
